in_text_mentions: The reduction in AAD and improvement of clinical symptoms were achieved for all patients in this study (Figs. 4, 5). We consider C2 subfacetal screws to be a neglected alternative to pedicle screws for the management of patients KFS. The C2 subfacetal screw technique is simple and safe. The dural membrane can be observed directly inside the insertion point, and the risk of spinal cord injury is low. The insertion point is located above the VA and there is no risk of VA injury. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Coronal CT reformat of the craniocervical junction from the Klippel-Feil syndrome case report, showing C2-C3 vertebral assimilation (fusion), platybasia with the odontoid process above the bimastoid line (basilar invagination), and atlantooccipital assimilation — all well-recognized skeletal manifestations of KFS. B: Sagittal CT reformat of the craniocervical junction from the KFS case report, demonstrating platybasia (skull base angle 155 degrees) with the odontoid process 25 mm above the Chamberlain line (basilar invagination) and assimilation/fusion of C2 and C3 — characteristic craniocervical bony abnormalities of Klippel-Feil syndrome.

in_text_mentions: A 75‐year‐old woman was referred to our hospital with intraventricular hemorrhage (Fig. 1) caused by hypertensive choroid plexus hemorrhage. She had a history of hearing loss from childhood. Cranial magnetic resonance (MR) imaging at age 73 years for screening of dementia demonstrated ventricular enlargement (Fig. 2A). On admission, she had mild conscious disturbance (Glasgow Coma Scale [GCS] 12: E = 4, V = 3, M = 5), gait disorder, and difficulty in feeding herself. She had short neck and low posterior hairline (Fig. 3A,B).

Radiography showed fusion of the cervical vertebrae at C2–4 and C5–7 (Fig. 3C,D). Cranial computed tomography and MR imaging demonstrated enlargement of the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles, and slight ballooning of the floor of the third ventricle. No indications of mass lesion were detected (Fig. 1B). The posterior cranial fossa volume measured by MR imaging was 145.4 mL. Based on these findings, the diagnosis was obstructive hydrocephalus associated with Klippel–Feil syndrome, with the suspected obstruction located at the outlet of the fourth ventricle.

panels.rationale: Sagittal MRI of the cervical spine from a patient with Klippel-Feil syndrome (per the article title 'Severe Klippel-Feil syndrome with Mondini malformation of inner ear' and the caption). The image shows fused vertebral bodies throughout the cervical spine — the defining radiological manifestation of Klippel-Feil syndrome — together with absent posterior elements, severe hyperextension and splitting of the cervical cord. This is a real human-patient radiology image of the configured disease with clear caption-triad support; no other disease, control, diagram or third-party material is involved. Extensive whole-cervical fusion with hyperextension and cord splitting represents a recognized severe (less common) form rather than the usual one- or two-segment fusion, hence variant; no subtype (e.g., Type I/II/III) is stated in the caption or text, so subtype is null.
